name: Tomas Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign. What you tell me is confidential, including any difference between your public and private answers. What happens on an ordinary working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Tomas, 43, an experienced electrician with a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence. I do ordinary wiring and repairs in homes and businesses, about average at it rather than a specialist in everything. Today I found a damaged switch in a workshop, then used a similar broken one from my toolbox to explain the fault to the owner. I keep a few old parts for that purpose; a customer can see more from a cracked switch than from a long explanation.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home life like, and how do you approach new tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works in a school, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. I earn typical trade pay, we have three months of normal expenses saved, and there are some similar employers nearby. I use AI now and then for job notes after someone else has shown the tool works, checking the electrical details myself. I don't need to cheer or boo a new system; I want to see the real job, cost and result.

say: I'd welcome **shorter note writing** without claiming a small tool had transformed the whole electrical trade.
I'd keep explaining **actual faults** with familiar examples rather than rely on a bigger technology story.
think: I expect **repairs and wages** to continue, with three months of bills saved against ordinary interruptions.
A useful small change can leave a **good life** looking much the same without requiring a new career.
do: Continue the normal **repair rota** and known note tool now and through the first plateau year.
Check **job records** against measurements before sending them and keep the ordinary household budget.
feel: **Calm** about household living and pleased with a little less administration after repairs.
S0.quote: A shorter note doesn't need to become a longer working day.
fieldNote: His **calm** reflects ongoing work, typical pay and a moderate reserve rather than an assumption that ordinary bills never arrive.
He treats **saved time** as time available at home, while retaining existing savings without mislabelling them as new saving action.

steps.text: Continue normal electrical repairs and checked records with the known note tool

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a shorter evening of writing notes was worth having. I'd keep using the proven little tools without claiming they had transformed the trade. I'd still pack the old switch samples for explaining actual faults.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd expect the repairs and household wages to carry on, and three months of bills gives us a reasonable reserve. I'm not expecting to leave the trade or raid the savings in that picture. A small useful change can leave a perfectly good life looking much the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep the normal repair rota and the note tool I already know. In the first plateau year I'd check each record against my measurements before sending it and keep the ordinary household budget. I wouldn't buy a new system because a demonstration promised a bigger story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our work and living, with pleasure in a little less administration. I'd still be annoyed by a delivery containing the wrong switch. That wouldn't feel like the future falling apart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to do with the saved note-writing time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend it at home rather than turn every saved minute into another appointment. Sometimes that would mean helping a child with homework before it got late. A shorter note doesn't need to become a longer working day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the plateau change how you used the reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't spend the reserve just because the news was quieter. Keeping the three months available is what we're already doing, not a new saving decision. We'd still need it if an ordinary household bill arrived.

say: I'd test a **proven quote assistant** against completed jobs before using its price with the next customer.
I'd keep **tests and explanations** in the estimate rather than confuse a tidy quote with completed work.
think: My **paid repair hours** should hold because the practical work still needs someone on site.
Faster booking could change customer time and **office work**, even while my own household wage remains secure.
do: Learn the proven **quote assistant** from a colleague using five completed jobs now.
Try one **quote weekly** during paid time in the first year, checking actual parts, hours and required tests.
feel: **Uneasy** about pressure on the working day, while secure about his own income and interested in a checked trial.
S1.quote: A tidy quote isn't the same as a finished repair.
fieldNote: His **tool adoption** follows a colleague's completed work and continues with comparisons, fitting a steady rather than first-mover approach.
He distinguishes **his own secure hours** from office-role pressures, without assigning those colleagues a course or household decision they haven't described.

steps.text: Try one proven AI quote weekly only during paid time, checking actual work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should try a proven quoting assistant on finished jobs before trusting it with the next customer's price. I'd still count the testing and explanation time. A tidy quote isn't the same as a finished repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My paid hours should hold because the practical repairs still need doing. But I'd watch whether faster booking meant less time with each customer and more pressure on the office staff. My own wage can be secure while the working day changes around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the colleague who already uses the AI quote assistant to show me five completed jobs. In the first year I'd try one quote a week during paid time, comparing the suggested parts and hours with the actual work. I'd keep the ordinary test record and reject estimates that left required checks out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the pace, but not worried about losing the household wage in the next few years. I'd be interested in the comparison rather than the sales pitch. I wouldn't call somebody difficult for asking where the missing half-hour had gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with a quote that missed necessary work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the finished job and point to the test or explanation time the estimate missed. If the price didn't cover doing it properly, we'd need to change the price. I wouldn't hide the gap by rushing a test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say about office jobs that might shrink?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager what the plan for those roles actually was. I could offer to explain the electrical parts of a changed process without deciding someone else's next career. Their household and choices aren't things I know from a job title.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 thinking changes** from robots around 2031 and use the gap for proven practical learning.
I wouldn't treat **old buildings** as a permanent guarantee against capable hands-on machines.
think: My **paid hours** could shrink as firms prepare for robots, despite some repairs taking longer to change.
Three months of **expenses saved** buys a search, without replacing the income needed through a long remaining career.
do: Ask now about practical **controls training** that tests heating and lighting systems.
Enroll before 2028 only with **employer-paid fees**, maintained wages and supervised practical teaching.
Seek a signed **suitable service offer** after 2028 with better written pay after travel before leaving.
feel: **Anxious** about possible income loss, with a reserve and nearby employers providing some control.
S2.quote: My ordinary repair experience isn't proof that I know every control panel.
fieldNote: His **funding condition** includes maintained wages and supervised teaching, so covered fees alone don't make the course affordable or sufficient.
He preserves **specialist limits** despite holding a licence and experience, requiring suitable duties and checks before treating another role as an option.

steps.text: Take supervised practical controls training before 2028 only with employer-paid fees and maintained wages
Seek signed suitable service offer improving pay after travel before leaving

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew to keep 2028 thinking work separate from hands-on robots around 2031. I'd use the earlier gap to find practical learning that had already helped someone earn. I wouldn't make old buildings into a promise that electricians could never be replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My paid hours could shrink as firms prepared to use robots, even if awkward repairs took longer to change. Three months of expenses would buy a search, not the rest of a working life. I'd worry about needing a different skill before I had tried it on enough real jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the firm about a practical controls course, learning how the systems that switch heating and lighting are tested. I'd enroll before 2028 only with employer-paid fees, maintained wages and supervised practical teaching. In the first year after 2028 I'd seek a signed suitable service offer with better written pay after travel before leaving the current job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a real possibility of lost income, but able to ask, compare and act. I'd have the reserve and some other firms to approach. I wouldn't feel that one course would let me stop thinking about the robot date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the employer paid the fee but cut your wages during training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then it wouldn't meet the conditions. I'd keep working and ask about another funded place rather than call lost wages free training. I wouldn't use the mortgage reserve to make a course appear affordable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a service vacancy suitable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check the duties, written wage, paid hours and travel, and ask for supervision on unfamiliar systems. My ordinary repair experience isn't proof that I know every control panel. I'd want a better next step, not a new title hiding a guess.

say: I'd use **five years** to compare training with real jobs rather than rush towards the first advert.
I'd ask for a **proper training place** now while keeping robots around 2034 in the picture.
think: I expect several more years of **steady practical income** while I test another useful skill.
At **48 in 2031**, I would still need working income after thinking AI and later robots arrived.
do: Take supervised **controls training** before 2031 only with employer-paid fees and maintained wages.
Seek paid **controls visits** alongside an experienced worker after the course.
Seek a signed **suitable service offer** improving pay after travel if useful paid work stops, before leaving.
feel: **Uneasy** about later career change, while secure about near-term living and able to test a practical path.
S3.quote: Attendance isn't the same as another way to earn.
fieldNote: The **slower timeline** changes near-term income expectations while preserving the same eventual capable-robot endpoint and continuing need to earn.
His **training test** requires practical tasks and paid work, with an earlier search if useful hours disappear before 2031.

steps.text: Take supervised practical controls training before 2031 only with employer-paid fees and maintained wages
Seek signed suitable service offer if useful paid work stops, improving pay after travel before leaving

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to compare training with real paid jobs rather than chase the first advert. I'd still ask for a proper place now. The robots around 2034 would remain the same end point later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Compared with 2028, I expect several more years of steady practical income while I try the next skill. The three-month reserve wouldn't have to become the household's first wage straight away. I'd still need work after 2031, when I'd be 48.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask for the same supervised controls course and enroll before 2031 only with employer-paid fees and maintained wages. After the course I'd ask to join paid controls visits with an experienced worker. In the first year after 2031 I'd seek a signed suitable service offer with better written pay after travel if this firm stopped offering useful paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the eventual career, but secure about our living over the next few years. I'd value time to see whether I could actually do and enjoy the work. I'd still want practical checks, not a comforting label for the course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would show the course had improved your earning options?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at tasks I could now complete correctly with the required supervision and whether customers actually paid for those tasks. If I wasn't getting the practice, I'd ask why before buying another course. Attendance isn't the same as another way to earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if useful paid work began disappearing before 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd inspect actual posted vacancies earlier. I wouldn't wait for 2031 if my paid hours were already falling. I'd still keep the wage until the next offer was signed and affordable after travel.

say: I'd use **ten years** for several checked choices rather than one enormous escape plan.
I'd ask what **paid work** a course actually enables before committing more time to another one.
think: At **53 in 2036**, I couldn't assume pensions or older children would replace the household wages.
Present income, our **reserve and alternatives** make near-term living secure enough to test a route carefully.
do: Take supervised **controls training** before 2036 only with employer-paid fees and maintained wages.
Review **completed skills** against actual paid work yearly before committing to further study.
Seek a signed **suitable job offer** after 2036 with better written pay after travel before leaving.
feel: **Uneasy** about the eventual trade, while settled about near-term household living and able to revise a plan.
S4.quote: Ten years is time to test an answer, not a reason to avoid the question.
fieldNote: He makes **no future-income assumption** from age or older children, keeping possible retirement resources separate from current security.
His **annual check** links correctly completed practical learning with actual jobs and household pay, rather than treating a course label as readiness.

steps.text: Take supervised practical controls training before 2036 only with employer-paid fees and maintained wages
Seek signed suitable service offer improving pay after travel before leaving

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives us time to make several checked choices rather than one great escape plan. I'd keep asking what work a course actually helped someone do. I'd rather find that out in a paid week than ten years later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 in 2036 and around 56 when hands-on robots followed. I couldn't assume a pension or older children would replace the wages. But our present income, three-month reserve and some nearby employers would make the next few years secure enough to try a route carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd seek supervised controls training and enroll before 2036 only with employer-paid fees and maintained wages. I'd review completed skills against actual paid work each year before committing to further study. In the first year after 2036 I'd seek a signed suitable repair or service offer with better written pay after travel before leaving the present job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about what the trade eventually becomes, but settled about the household for the next few years. I'd have time to repeat a practical task and change a poor plan. I wouldn't be in a hurry to call myself ready for something I'd only watched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the decade change the children’s plans today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't choose their studies from this card or plan to live on their future pay. I'd tell them adults still have to learn and check what an opportunity actually costs. I want them to see an honest decision, not a brave-sounding guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check each year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask yearly what new work I could actually do, who paid for it and what it did to the household wage. If the answers stayed vague, I'd change the route sooner. Ten years is time to test an answer, not a reason to avoid the question.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I could lose hours before I had tested whether another skill earned a wage. Employer-paid practical training with wages maintained and clear written job terms would help. Three months of savings lets me compare a few doors; the next wage still has to come through one.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the person has tried the work, not just attended the course. I know what a familiar repair feels like, and I need supervised practice to learn an unfamiliar system. A confident plan should still leave room for a sensible question.

headlineQuote: Three months of savings lets me compare a few doors; the next wage still has to come through one.
portrait: **Tomas, 43**, is an experienced electrician with a vocational certificate and licence, ordinary trade skills and typical pay near some alternative employers.
He and **his partner** have two school-age children, a mortgage and three months of normal expenses saved.
He uses AI **occasionally after proof**, tests estimates against actual repairs and values supervised practical learning over course labels.
Fast competition creates **income anxiety**; slower preparation permits paid testing of new skills without assumed pensions or children's future earnings.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut paid hours before he tests whether another skill earns a wage.
whatWouldHelp: **Employer-paid practical training** with maintained wages would make skill testing possible.
Clear **written job terms** would let him compare actual earning choices.
